propositions.text: Once the Crown establishes certain conditions, the burden shifts to the accused to raise a reasonable doubt about breathalyzer test reliability.
propositions.quote: once the Crown has established certain conditions, the burden shifts to the accused to raise a reasonable doubt about the reliability of the breathalyzer test results.

propositions.text: If no evidence raises a doubt, breathalyzer results are presumed accurate and reflect the accused's blood alcohol at the time of testing and the material time.
propositions.quote: If there is no evidence raising such a doubt, the results are presumed to be accurate, which is to say that the alcohol level in the breath sample is presumed to reflect the alcohol level in the accused’s blood at the time of testing, and that level is presumed to be identical to the alcohol level in the accused’s blood at the material time.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the burden-shifting framework for breathalyzer evidence and the resulting presumptions if the accused raises no doubt.

propositions.text: The appeal concerns what evidence is needed to rebut breathalyzer presumptions under s. 258(1)(c) of the Criminal Code.
propositions.quote: This appeal concerns the scope of the evidence that must be adduced to rebut the presumptions of accuracy and identity that are applicable to breathalyzer test results under s. 258(1) (c) of the Criminal Code

propositions.text: The Court allowed the Crown’s appeal, set aside the acquittal, and ordered a new trial, with reasons to follow.
propositions.quote: the Court allowed the Crown’s appeal from the judgment of the Court of Appeal, set aside the verdict of acquittal restored by the Court of Appeal, and ordered a new trial, with reasons to follow.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the appeal concerns the evidence needed to rebut breathalyzer presumptions and notes it allowed the Crown's appeal and ordered a new trial.

propositions.text: To rebut s. 258(1)(c) presumptions, the accused must show malfunction or improper operation casts doubt on reliability.
propositions.quote: an accused must adduce evidence tending to show that the malfunctioning or improper operation of the approved instrument casts doubt on the reliability of the results

propositions.text: Evidence must relate directly to deficiencies in maintenance or operation of the instrument.
propositions.quote: What the new provisions require is that evidence tending to cast doubt on the reliability of the results relate directly to such deficiencies.

propositions.text: This requirement ensures scientific recognition of results and promotes proper functioning and operation of instruments.
propositions.quote: First, it aims to ensure continued scientific recognition of breathalyzer test results, and second, it promotes the proper functioning and proper operation of instruments in order to prevent the reliability of the results from being compromised

paragraphs.summary: The court explains that to rebut breathalyzer presumptions, evidence must show improper operation casts doubt on reliability and must relate to specific deficiencies.

propositions.text: The accused must adduce evidence of improper operation and show the defect tends to cast doubt on reliability.
propositions.quote: The accused’s burden is discharged if the following conditions are met: (i) the accused adduces evidence relating directly to the malfunctioning or improper operation of the instrument, and (ii) the accused establishes that this defect tends to cast doubt on the reliability of the results.

propositions.text: Each condition has theoretical and practical elements: a required procedure and proof it was not followed; and proof the defect could affect reliability.
propositions.quote: Each of these conditions has a theoretical element and a practical element. Therefore, for the improper operation of the instrument to be established, it must first be found that a specific procedure is generally required (theoretical element), and it must then be shown that the procedure was not in fact followed (practical element).

propositions.text: The purpose of the procedure must be to ensure reliability, and evidence must show the defect could have affected reliability in the case.
propositions.quote: The theoretical element is satisfied where it is proved that the purpose of the procedure in question is to ensure the reliability of the results. On the practical element, the evidence must establish that, in the particular case, the defect could have affected the reliability of the results.

paragraphs.summary: The court outlines the two-part burden on the accused: show improper operation and that it could affect reliability, each with theoretical and practical elements.

propositions.text: There is no need to address whether improper operation was established; even if assumed, no evidence showed it tended to cast doubt on reliability.
propositions.quote: Even if we assume, without deciding, that improper operation of the instrument was established here based on failure to complete the 15‑ or 20‑minute observation period, there was clearly no evidence that this improper operation tended to cast doubt on the reliability of the results.

propositions.text: The Court of Appeal’s judgment must be reversed and the Superior Court’s judgment ordering a new trial restored.
propositions.quote: The Court of Appeal’s judgment must be reversed. The Superior Court’s judgment setting aside the verdict of acquittal by the Court of Québec and ordering a new trial must be restored.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no evidence that improper operation cast doubt on reliability and orders the Superior Court's new trial decision restored.

propositions.text: On July 12, 2012, Marc Cyr-Langlois was stopped, arrested, searched, and taken to the police station.
propositions.quote: On July 12, 2012, the respondent Marc Cyr‑Langlois was stopped by Constables Boissonneault and Cousineau while he was driving his vehicle. Constable Cousineau arrested him at around 12:35 a.m. The respondent was frisk searched and then taken to the police station.

propositions.text: At the station, the officers and respondent were in adjacent rooms; Boissonneault prepared the breathalyzer, Cousineau observed respondent during his call to counsel.
propositions.quote: When they arrived at the station at around 12:54 a.m., the three men went into two adjacent rooms separated by a window. Constable Boissonneault, a qualified technician, went into the breathalyzer room to prepare the instrument and run a control test. Constable Cousineau accompanied the respondent to the interrogation room and then joined Constable Boissonneault in the adjacent breathalyzer room while the respondent exercised his right to counsel confidentially. Constable Cousineau observed the respondent through the window while he placed a call to his counsel, which ended at around 1:05 a.m.

paragraphs.summary: The court describes the events of July 12, 2012, including the respondent's arrest, search, and observation at the police station.

propositions.text: At 1:08 a.m., the first breathalyzer test showed 157 mg/100 ml; at 1:30 a.m., the second showed 148 mg/100 ml.
propositions.quote: At 1:08 a.m., Constable Boissonneault gave the respondent a first breathalyzer test, which showed 157 mg of alcohol in 100 ml of blood. ... At 1:30 a.m., Constable Boissonneault administered the second breathalyzer test, which showed 148 mg of alcohol in 100 ml of blood.

propositions.text: Both results were over the legal limit, with less than 10 mg difference; respondent was charged with two offences, only the second is at issue.
propositions.quote: Both results were therefore over the legal limit, with a difference of less than 10 mg. The respondent was then charged with operating a motor vehicle while his ability to do so was impaired by alcohol and with operating a motor vehicle with a blood alcohol level exceeding 80 mg of alcohol in 100 ml of blood. Only the second charge is in issue here.

paragraphs.summary: The court details the breathalyzer results and charges, noting only the over-80 charge is at issue.

propositions.text: At trial, parties agreed the court should first decide if Boissonneault breached duty by not observing accused for 15 or 20 minutes before each test.
propositions.quote: the parties agreed that the court should begin by determining whether Constable Boissonneault had breached the duty to operate the breathalyzer properly by failing to observe the accused himself for a period of 15 or 20 minutes before administering each test.

propositions.text: The accused argued that failure to observe for 15 or 20 minutes rebutted the presumptions and required acquittal absent further Crown evidence.
propositions.quote: The accused argued that, in such a case, the presumptions were rebutted, which had to lead to his acquittal in the absence of additional evidence from the Crown.

paragraphs.summary: At trial, the parties focused on whether failure to observe the accused for 15 or 20 minutes rebutted the presumptions, as the accused argued.

propositions.text: Only Constable Boissonneault testified for the Crown; the trial judge decided from the bench.
propositions.quote: Only Constable Boissonneault testified for the Crown, and the trial judge rendered his decision from the bench.

propositions.text: The trial judge found the technician need not observe the accused himself, but Cousineau's observation was not continuous.
propositions.quote: The trial judge found that, while the technician was not required to observe the accused himself, the period during which Constable Cousineau had done so was not continuous.

propositions.text: The judge stated that not following the observation procedure was sufficient to raise a reasonable doubt, as its purpose is to ensure reliability.
propositions.quote: he then stated that, since the general purpose of the observation procedure is to ensure the reliability of the results, his finding that the procedure had not been followed in this case was sufficient to raise a reasonable doubt.

propositions.text: The judge acquitted the respondent of the second charge; the Crown had no evidence on the first charge.
propositions.quote: He therefore acquitted the respondent of the second charge, and the Crown stated that it had no evidence to adduce on the first charge.

paragraphs.summary: The trial judge found the observation was not continuous, held this was enough to raise doubt, and acquitted the respondent on the second charge.

propositions.text: The Crown appealed, arguing the evidence to rebut the presumptions was lacking; the Superior Court allowed the appeal and ordered a new trial.
propositions.quote: the Crown appealed as of right to the Superior Court, which allowed the appeal, set aside the judgment of acquittal and ordered a new trial.

propositions.text: Zigman J. found the trial judge did not properly apply the law and made a fatal error in acquitting the respondent.
propositions.quote: the trial judge did not properly apply the law and made a fatal error of law in acquitting the [respondent].

paragraphs.summary: The Superior Court allowed the Crown's appeal, finding the trial judge erred in law and ordering a new trial.

propositions.text: To rebut the presumptions, an accused must show a deficiency in operation and that it directly relates to reliability of the results.
propositions.quote: To rebut the statutory presumptions an accused must establish to the reasonable doubt standard: (a) a deficiency in the functioning or operation of the instrument; and (b) that the deficiency directly related to the reliability of the breath test results.

paragraphs.summary: The Alberta Court of Appeal in So set out that an accused must show a deficiency and its direct relation to reliability to rebut presumptions.

propositions.text: The respondent sought leave to appeal to the Court of Appeal, which was granted; the majority restored the acquittal.
propositions.quote: The respondent subsequently sought leave to appeal to the Court of Appeal on a question of law, which was granted. A majority of the Court of Appeal set aside the Superior Court’s judgment and restored the verdict of acquittal.

propositions.text: All judges agreed the accused must show improper operation and adduce evidence tending to show it could influence the result.
propositions.quote: All of the judges agreed that an accused must not only establish that the breathalyzer was operated improperly, but must also adduce evidence tending to show that its improper operation [translation] “[could] influence the result”

propositions.text: The majority found this was a question of fact and the Superior Court erred in intervening absent an unreasonable assessment by the trial judge.
propositions.quote: the majority found that this determination essentially concerned a question of fact and that the Superior Court had erred in intervening absent an unreasonable assessment of the evidence by the trial judge.

propositions.text: The dissenting judge would have upheld the Superior Court, finding no evidence of a deficiency that could affect the result.
propositions.quote: The dissenting judge would have upheld the Superior Court’s decision on the ground that “[t]he [Court of Québec] judge was not faced with evidence showing a deficiency [that could] affect the result”

paragraphs.summary: The Court of Appeal restored the acquittal, with all judges agreeing on the need for evidence the defect could influence results; the dissent disagreed on the facts.

propositions.text: The issue is how an accused can show improper operation casts doubt on reliability, and whether theoretical evidence suffices.
propositions.quote: The heart of the dispute comes down to the following: is evidence that is purely theoretical sufficient for this purpose?

paragraphs.summary: The court frames the issue as whether theoretical evidence is enough to show improper operation casts doubt on reliability.

propositions.text: Abstract evidence alone may sometimes suffice, but more concrete evidence is usually required to raise a reasonable doubt.
propositions.quote: it is more likely that evidence that relates more concretely to the facts in issue will be required. This was the case here: without such evidence, the accused’s argument was in the realm of speculation and could not satisfy the reasonable doubt test

paragraphs.summary: The court finds that, in this case, only concrete evidence could satisfy the reasonable doubt test, not mere speculation.

propositions.text: It was not enough to show the defect could theoretically compromise reliability; mere hypothetical possibility is insufficient to raise a reasonable doubt.
propositions.quote: Relying on such evidence amounts to accepting a [translation] “mere hypothetical possibility”, which is clearly not sufficient to raise a reasonable doubt

propositions.text: The respondent was searched twice, monitored, and the test results were consistent, so any digestive issue would have had to affect both tests similarly.
propositions.quote: the respondent was searched twice, that he was monitored by the police officers and that the two test results were consistent, which means that if there was a digestive issue that had a distorting effect, it must have occurred before each test and affected each result in the same way.

propositions.text: The improper operation alleged did not tend to show reliability was in doubt; the minimum evidence required was not adduced.
propositions.quote: the mere improper operation alleged by the respondent did not in itself tend to show that the reliability of the results was in doubt. The minimum evidence required for this purpose was simply not adduced.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds theoretical evidence is insufficient, and the facts do not support a reasonable doubt about reliability in this case.

propositions.text: Improper operation may sometimes be so serious or closely connected to reliability that it alone raises a reasonable doubt.
propositions.quote: I do not rule out the possibility that improper operation may be so serious or so closely connected with reliability that it will be sufficient in itself to raise a reasonable doubt about the reliability of the results obtained.

propositions.text: What matters is that the defect's possible impact on reliability is serious enough to raise a reasonable doubt, regardless of how it is inferred.
propositions.quote: What is essential is that the possibility that the defect affected the reliability of the results is serious enough to raise a reasonable doubt.

propositions.text: Concrete evidence must link improper operation or malfunction to the results; mere hypothesis or conjecture is insufficient.
propositions.quote: Although expert evidence is not essential, concrete evidence must be tendered to show that the improper operation or malfunctioning of the instrument may be linked to the results (as opposed to the necessity to show that improper operation did in fact lead to unreliable results). In sum, the evidence should not be mere hypothesis or conjecture.

propositions.text: The trial judge did not point to any concrete evidence; the evidence showed nothing beyond conjecture and speculation.
propositions.quote: The Court of Québec judge did not point to any concrete evidence in this regard, and for good reason: beyond conjecture and speculation, the evidence showed nothing.

propositions.text: Zigman J. correctly found no evidence tending to cast doubt on reliability; the Court of Appeal majority erred in reversing him.
propositions.quote: Zigman J. of the Superior Court correctly found that there was no evidence tending to cast doubt on the reliability of the results, and the majority of the Court of Appeal erred in reversing his decision.

paragraphs.summary: The court holds only serious or closely connected defects may suffice, but here there was no concrete evidence linking the defect to reliability.

propositions.text: The intervener argues an accused cannot testify about alcohol consumption or digestive problems without contravening s. 258(1)(d.01) Cr. C.
propositions.quote: An intervener, the Criminal Lawyers’ Association, argues that it would be impossible for an accused to testify about his or her alcohol consumption or digestive problems without contravening s. 258(1) (d.01) Cr. C.

propositions.text: The intervener is mistaken; an accused may testify about digestive problems to provide concrete evidence affecting reliability after identifying a deficiency.
propositions.quote: The intervener is mistaken. ... an accused who testifies to establish that he or she had a digestive problem is not seeking thereby to show that the instrument was operated improperly. Rather, the accused is providing concrete, rational evidence that the reliability of the results may have been affected, after first identifying a deficiency in the operation of the instrument. This distinction is crucial.

propositions.text: Such testimonial evidence is admissible but not compulsory.
propositions.quote: Of course, the fact that such testimonial evidence is admissible does not make it compulsory.

paragraphs.summary: The court rejects the intervener's argument, clarifying that accuseds may testify about digestive issues to provide concrete evidence affecting reliability.

propositions.text: The respondent maintains he did not present a 'burping defence' as it relates only to s. 258(1)(d.1) Cr. C.
propositions.quote: the respondent, who maintains that he did not present a “burping defence” because that defence relates solely to s. 258(1) (d.1) Cr. C.

propositions.text: The burping defence was essential to the respondent's arguments, as he claimed improper operation cast doubt due to possible unnoticed digestive issues.
propositions.quote: The burping defence was an essential part of his arguments. He argued that the improper operation of the instrument cast doubt on the reliability of the results precisely because, in such a case, the police might not notice certain digestive issues that can have a distorting effect: the discussion during the hearing before the Court of Québec judge confirms that this question was central to the respondent’s submissions.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the respondent's arguments did rely on a 'burping defence' related to possible unnoticed digestive issues affecting reliability.

propositions.text: There was no evidence tending to show the alleged defect cast doubt on reliability; the defect could not form the basis for reasonable doubt.
propositions.quote: there was absolutely no evidence tending to show that the alleged defect cast doubt on the reliability of the results. That defect therefore could not form the basis for a reasonable doubt.

propositions.text: Acceptance of theoretical evidence based on speculation misinterprets the accused’s burden and is an error of law.
propositions.quote: acceptance of theoretical evidence based on speculation reflects a misinterpretation of the accused’s burden of proof, which is an error of law.

propositions.text: The Superior Court did not err in setting aside the acquittal and ordering a new trial.
propositions.quote: The Superior Court did not err in setting aside the respondent’s acquittal and ordering a new trial.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no evidence the defect cast doubt on reliability, holds speculation is an error of law, and upholds the new trial order.

propositions.text: The evidentiary scheme for over-80 offences infringes s. 11(d) Charter rights, justified partly by breathalyzer reliability.
propositions.quote: the evidentiary scheme applicable to offences involving driving with a blood alcohol level over the legal limit infringes the right to be presumed innocent guaranteed by s. 11 (d) of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms . One reason why this infringement is justified in part is because of the recognized reliability of breathalyzer test results.

propositions.text: Reliability of results depends on proper functioning and operation; if a reasonable doubt is raised, s. 258(1)(c) presumptions must be discarded.
propositions.quote: the reliability of the results is itself contingent on the proper functioning and proper operation of the instrument. Where an accused raises a reasonable doubt in this regard, there is no longer any basis for the presumptions of accuracy and identity created by s. 258(1) (c) of the Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C‑46 (“Cr. C.”),[1] and those presumptions must be discarded.

paragraphs.summary: The court cites precedent that the over-80 evidentiary scheme infringes Charter rights, justified by reliability, which depends on proper operation.

propositions.text: The trial judge found the qualified technician’s testimony showed the observation period before the breathalyzer test was not complied with.
propositions.quote: the trial judge found that the qualified technician’s testimony tended to show that the observation period required prior to the administration of the breathalyzer test had not been complied with

propositions.text: This was sufficient to raise a reasonable doubt about the reliability of the results and deprive the prosecution of the statutory presumptions.
propositions.quote: this was sufficient to raise a reasonable doubt about the reliability of the results and thus to deprive the prosecution of the benefit of the statutory presumptions

propositions.text: The trial judge made no error of law warranting appellate intervention.
propositions.quote: the trial judge made no error of law that would warrant appellate intervention

propositions.text: The issue is one of weighing evidence, so the acquittal must be upheld.
propositions.quote: The issue is ultimately one of weighing of evidence, and the acquittal must therefore be upheld.

paragraphs.summary: The trial judge found the observation period was not followed, raising reasonable doubt, and the court finds no legal error, so the acquittal stands.

propositions.text: Requiring evidence that improper operation actually led to inaccurate results would upset the balance between accuseds' rights and Parliament’s objectives.
propositions.quote: To require, as the majority does in practice, evidence tending to show that the improper operation of the breathalyzer in fact led to inaccurate results ... would upset the delicate balance between the constitutional rights of accused persons and Parliament’s objectives.

propositions.text: Combined with Gubbins, such a requirement would make defences supporting the constitutionality of the evidentiary scheme illusory.
propositions.quote: such a requirement would render even more illusory the defences on which the constitutionality of the evidentiary scheme at issue in St‑Onge Lamoureux depends.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds that requiring proof of actual inaccuracy would undermine accuseds' rights and make constitutional defences illusory, especially after Gubbins.

propositions.text: The court will discuss St-Onge Lamoureux, clarify burdens regarding breathalyzer operation, review the facts, and address fairness of a new trial.
propositions.quote: I will briefly discuss this Court’s reasoning in St‑Onge Lamoureux. Then, I will provide some clarification concerning the respective burdens of the defence and the Crown with regard to the functioning and operation of the breathalyzer. I will then consider the facts of this case in order to demonstrate that the original verdict of acquittal is, in my view, unimpeachable. Lastly, I will conclude by emphasizing that it would be unfair to order a new trial given the fact that the Crown is relying on arguments made for the first time on appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The court outlines its plan: discuss St-Onge Lamoureux, clarify burdens, review facts, and address fairness of ordering a new trial.

propositions.text: The appeal requires considering the accused's burden to counter s. 258(1)(c) presumptions and the evidence needed to discharge it.
propositions.quote: this appeal requires the Court to consider the burden resting on an accused who seeks to counter the presumptions of accuracy and identity in s. 258(1) (c) Cr. C. as well as the type of evidence that the accused must adduce to discharge that burden.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the appeal concerns the accused's burden to counter statutory presumptions and the evidence required to do so.

propositions.text: The court’s position is based on the majority in St-Onge Lamoureux, as in Gubbins.
propositions.quote: My position is based, as it was in the recent decision in Gubbins, on the majority reasons in St‑Onge Lamoureux.

propositions.text: The majority acknowledges St-Onge Lamoureux’s relevance but departs from it.
propositions.quote: the majority also acknowledges the relevance of St‑Onge Lamoureux, but in my view, and with respect, it departs from that decision.

propositions.text: St-Onge Lamoureux upheld the evidentiary scheme partly because accuseds could still counter presumptions by raising reasonable doubt about proper operation.
propositions.quote: there was still a real possibility that the accused could counter the statutory presumptions by raising a reasonable doubt about the proper operation of the breathalyzer.

paragraphs.summary: The court relies on St-Onge Lamoureux, notes the majority departs from it, and cites its rationale for upholding the evidentiary scheme.

propositions.text: Scientific evidence in St-Onge Lamoureux showed breathalyzers are reliable but require faithful adherence to procedures for accuracy.
propositions.quote: the scientific evidence adduced in St‑Onge Lamoureux demonstrated the reliability of breathalyzers, it also highlighted the importance of following the relevant procedures faithfully in order to obtain accurate results

propositions.text: Instrument malfunction or improper use is a real possibility, not merely speculative.
propositions.quote: The expert evidence filed in the instant case reveals that the possibility of an instrument malfunctioning or being used improperly when breath samples are taken is not merely speculative, but is very real.

propositions.text: Proper operation and maintenance by qualified personnel using good laboratory practice is essential for scientifically sound results.
propositions.quote: to achieve scientifically sound results in operational use, user agencies must ensure that approved instruments are operated by qualified personnel using procedures based on good laboratory practice.

paragraphs.summary: St-Onge Lamoureux found breathalyzers reliable if procedures are followed, but malfunctions are possible and proper operation is essential for accuracy.

propositions.text: The Alcohol Test Committee recommends a 15-minute observation period before collecting a breath sample.
propositions.quote: The Committee states that before collecting a breath sample, the qualified technician must, among other things, observe the test subject for 15 minutes

paragraphs.summary: The Alcohol Test Committee recommends a 15-minute observation period before breath sample collection to ensure reliability.

propositions.text: The constitutionality of the provisions depends partly on how possible and easy it is for the accused to rebut the presumption.
propositions.quote: the constitutionality of the provisions at issue depended, among other things, on “whether it is possible, and how easy it is, for the accused to rebut the presumption”

paragraphs.summary: The constitutionality of the evidentiary scheme depends on the accused's ability to rebut the presumption.

propositions.text: Only the first requirement—evidence tending to show malfunction or improper operation—was a reasonable limit on the presumption of innocence.
propositions.quote: only the first of the three requirements imposed on the accused by s. 258(1) (c) Cr. C. — that of adducing evidence tending to show that the instrument was malfunctioning or was operated improperly — constituted a reasonable limit on the right to be presumed innocent

propositions.text: This burden is justified because results are reliable only if instruments are operated and maintained properly.
propositions.quote: This burden was justified because it reflected the fact that “the results will be reliable only if the instruments are operated and maintained properly”

paragraphs.summary: St-Onge Lamoureux found only the first requirement—a showing of malfunction or improper operation—was a justified limit on the presumption of innocence.

propositions.text: The Court did not specify the evidence needed to show improper operation but noted the relevance of Alcohol Test Committee recommendations.
propositions.quote: The Court declined to specifically determine the nature and scope of the evidence required to show that the instrument was operated improperly (para. 42). However, Deschamps J. made a point of noting the relevance of the recommendations made by the Alcohol Test Committee of the Canadian Society of Forensic Science

propositions.text: Failure to follow recommended procedures may mean instruments do not function optimally.
propositions.quote: It can be inferred from these recommendations that the instruments may not function optimally if the suggested procedures are not followed.

paragraphs.summary: The Court did not define the evidence needed for improper operation but highlighted the importance of following recommended procedures.

propositions.text: If the accused shows relevant procedures were not followed, reliability cannot be assumed, justifying the first requirement under s. 1 of the Charter.
propositions.quote: it was possible for the accused to show that the relevant procedures had not been followed — in which case the reliability of the results could not be assumed — that the Court ultimately concluded that the first requirement imposed by s. 258(1) (c) Cr. C. was justified under s. 1 of the Charter

propositions.text: That conclusion clarifies the accused’s burden to counter statutory presumptions.
propositions.quote: that conclusion sheds light on the burden resting on an accused who seeks to counter the statutory presumptions.

paragraphs.summary: If procedures are not followed, reliability is not assumed, clarifying the accused's burden to counter statutory presumptions.

propositions.text: St-Onge Lamoureux did not make recommended breathalyzer procedures statutory conditions for the Crown to benefit from presumptions.
propositions.quote: I am not suggesting that St‑Onge Lamoureux elevated the various recommendations concerning the operation of breathalyzers — including that there be a period of observation of the accused — to the level of statutory conditions that the Crown must meet to benefit from the presumptions of accuracy and identity in s. 258(1) (c) Cr. C.

propositions.text: The only statutory conditions are those in s. 258(1)(c)(ii) to (iv).
propositions.quote: The only applicable statutory conditions are those imposed by Parliament in s. 258(1) (c)(ii) to (iv).

paragraphs.summary: The court clarifies that recommended procedures are not statutory conditions; only those in s. 258(1)(c)(ii)-(iv) apply.

propositions.text: The accused’s burden is only to adduce evidence tending to show malfunction or improper operation that could affect reliability, not actual inaccuracy.
propositions.quote: an accused who seeks to counter the statutory presumptions bears only the burden of adducing evidence tending to show a malfunction or improper operation of the breathalyzer that could affect the reliability of the results; the accused is not required to show that the results are in fact inaccurate

propositions.text: The evidence need only raise a reasonable doubt about reliability.
propositions.quote: It is also clear that the evidence in question need only raise a reasonable doubt in this regard

paragraphs.summary: The accused need only raise a reasonable doubt about reliability, not prove actual inaccuracy, to counter the presumptions.

propositions.text: St-Onge Lamoureux requires evidence of a defect that could cast doubt on reliability, consistent with R. v. So.
propositions.quote: St‑Onge Lamoureux, which simply requires evidence of a “defect that could cast doubt on the reliability of the results”

paragraphs.summary: St-Onge Lamoureux and R. v. So require only evidence of a defect that could cast doubt on reliability.

propositions.text: The Crown and majority accept the accused’s burden is to raise reasonable doubt about reliability by showing malfunction or improper operation.
propositions.quote: Like the Crown, the majority purports to accept that the burden on the accused is simply to raise a reasonable doubt about the reliability of the results by means of evidence tending to show that the breathalyzer was malfunctioning or was operated improperly

propositions.text: By requiring more concrete evidence, the majority imposes an obligation to cast doubt on accuracy, contrary to St-Onge Lamoureux.
propositions.quote: the majority is effectively imposing an obligation on the accused to cast doubt on the accuracy of the results on the facts of the case. With respect, I consider it contrary to this Court’s reasoning in St‑Onge Lamoureux to impose such a burden

propositions.text: St-Onge Lamoureux found the second requirement—demonstrating a connection between deficiency and results—was an unjustified infringement of the presumption of innocence.
propositions.quote: this Court held in St‑Onge Lamoureux that this second requirement — that of demonstrating a connection between the deficiency and the results indicating a blood alcohol level exceeding the legal limit — constituted a serious infringement of the right to be presumed innocent that could not be justified

paragraphs.summary: The Crown and majority accept a reasonable doubt standard, but the court finds the majority's approach wrongly requires proof of inaccuracy, contrary to precedent.

propositions.text: St-Onge Lamoureux requires evidence raising doubt about reliability, not accuracy, and these terms have different meanings.
propositions.quote: St‑Onge Lamoureux requires evidence that raises a reasonable doubt about the reliability rather than the accuracy of the results. These two terms, though related, do not have the same meaning.

propositions.text: Reliability means the ability to function without incident; accuracy means conformity to the truth.
propositions.quote: The former refers, in its technical sense, to the [translation] “[a]bility of a system . . . to function without incident for a period of time” and, by extension, to the “[n]ature of [something that can be relied on]” ... The latter refers to “[c]onformity to the truth”

propositions.text: The distinction between reliability and accuracy is significant.
propositions.quote: In my opinion, this distinction is significant.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains St-Onge Lamoureux requires doubt about reliability, not accuracy, and clarifies the important distinction between the two terms.

propositions.text: If evidence shows improper operation increased the possibility of inaccuracy, reliability is affected and the accused meets their burden.
propositions.quote: where the evidence tends to show — on the reasonable doubt standard — that the malfunctioning or improper operation of the breathalyzer increased the possibility of an inaccurate result, then reliability is affected and the accused has met his or her burden.

propositions.text: The accused need not provide additional evidence directly raising doubt about accuracy.
propositions.quote: The accused does not have to tender additional evidence in order to directly raise a reasonable doubt about the accuracy of the results on the facts of the case.

propositions.text: Evidence that a recommended procedure was not followed and its purpose is reliability suffices to meet the accused’s burden.
propositions.quote: it will be sufficient to adduce evidence tending to show that a recommended procedure was not faithfully followed and that the purpose of the procedure is to ensure the reliability of the results.

propositions.text: The accused’s burden ends there; the presumptions are justified only if procedures are complied with.
propositions.quote: The accused’s burden ends there, because the application of the presumptions in s. 258(1) (c) Cr. C. is justified only insofar as the relevant procedures are complied with

paragraphs.summary: The accused meets their burden by showing improper operation could affect reliability; no need for further evidence about accuracy.

propositions.text: The burden then shifts to the Crown to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the deficiency had no impact on accuracy.
propositions.quote: The burden then shifts to the Crown to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the deficiency in question had no impact on the accuracy of the results on the facts of the case.

propositions.text: St-Onge Lamoureux found this reverse onus is not excessive for the prosecution.
propositions.quote: there is nothing excessive about this reverse onus: “[B]eing the party that has to prove that there is no connection after the accused has adduced evidence to show that the instrument malfunctioned or was operated improperly does not impose a significant additional burden on the prosecution”

propositions.text: If the Crown fails, it loses the benefit of the statutory presumptions.
propositions.quote: if the Crown fails to discharge this burden, it completely loses the benefit of the statutory presumptions in s. 258(1) (c) Cr. C.

propositions.text: Mr. Cyr-Langlois argues the Crown should not rely on technician rigour for reliability and then trivialize it when challenged.
propositions.quote: The Crown should not be able to rely on the rigour of the technicians to persuade this Court that the results are reliable and then trivialize the importance of that rigour when the reliability of the results is challenged

paragraphs.summary: If the accused meets their burden, the Crown must prove no impact on accuracy; failure means losing presumptions, as Mr. Cyr-Langlois argues.

propositions.text: The accused may rely solely on the qualified technician’s testimony to raise reasonable doubt about reliability.
propositions.quote: There is nothing to prevent the accused from relying solely on the qualified technician’s testimony to raise a reasonable doubt about the reliability of the results.

propositions.text: Evidence to counter statutory presumptions may come from Crown or defence witnesses’ depositions.
propositions.quote: evidence to counter the statutory presumptions may be “sought in depositions given by witnesses of the Crown as well as in depositions of defence witnesses”

paragraphs.summary: The accused can use the qualified technician’s testimony alone to raise reasonable doubt, as evidence may come from any witness.

propositions.text: The qualified technician is responsible for proper operation of the breathalyzer under the Criminal Code.
propositions.quote: the qualified technician is responsible for the proper operation of the breathalyzer (see, for example, ss. 254(3) (a)(i) and 258(1) (c)(iv))

propositions.text: If the technician testifies a recommended procedure was not followed or is unsure, the accused need not provide further evidence to corroborate.
propositions.quote: the accused is not obliged to tender additional evidence — such as a copy of the training manual in issue — to corroborate the technician’s testimony

propositions.text: The technician’s testimony alone can raise a reasonable doubt about reliability.
propositions.quote: That testimony is in itself evidence that can raise a reasonable doubt about the reliability of the results.

propositions.text: To require more would disregard the unique role of qualified technicians in blood alcohol analysis.
propositions.quote: To take the opposite position would be to disregard the unique role conferred by Parliament on qualified technicians in the context of blood alcohol analysis.

paragraphs.summary: The technician’s testimony alone can raise reasonable doubt about reliability; no further corroboration is needed, given their statutory role.

propositions.text: It is for the trier of fact to assess the evidence adduced to determine whether it is sufficient to counter the statutory presumptions.
propositions.quote: It is for the trier of fact to assess the evidence adduced in order to determine whether it is sufficient to counter the statutory presumptions.

propositions.text: The trier of fact may find that the qualified technician’s testimony does not in itself raise a reasonable doubt if the problems identified are frivolous or trivial.
propositions.quote: the trier of fact may well find that, in the circumstances, the qualified technician’s testimony does not in itself raise a reasonable doubt, for example because the problems identified are “frivolous or trivial”

paragraphs.summary: The court states that the trier of fact decides if evidence counters statutory presumptions and may find technician testimony insufficient if issues are trivial.

propositions.text: The trial judge correctly stated the law and noted the accused must show breathalyzer malfunction or improper operation raising reasonable doubt about test reliability.
propositions.quote: The trial judge correctly stated the law. He properly noted that the accused must adduce evidence tending to show that the breathalyzer was malfunctioning or was operated improperly and that the deficiency in question must raise a reasonable doubt about the [translation] “reliability of the test taken”

propositions.text: The trial judge’s findings of fact are supported by the evidence adduced by the parties.
propositions.quote: His findings of fact on this point are supported by the evidence adduced by the parties.

propositions.text: The verdict of acquittal is unimpeachable.
propositions.quote: In my opinion, the verdict of acquittal is therefore unimpeachable.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the trial judge correctly stated the law, made supported findings, and that the acquittal verdict is unimpeachable.

propositions.text: The Crown has not identified any error of law warranting intervention by this Court.
propositions.quote: The Crown has not identified any error of law that would warrant this Court’s intervention.

propositions.text: The Crown argues it was deprived of the benefit of the presumptions due to a mere speculative possibility.
propositions.quote: Contrary to what it argues, it was deprived of the benefit of the presumptions in s. 258(1) (c) Cr. C. not because of a [translation] “mere speculative possibility”

propositions.text: The Crown lost the benefit of the presumptions due to concrete and specific evidence showing a relevant procedure was not followed, affecting reliability.
propositions.quote: but rather because of concrete and specific evidence showing that a relevant procedure — observation of the accused for a period of time — had not been followed and that this deficiency could affect the reliability of the results.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no legal error, rejects the Crown's argument of speculation, and finds concrete evidence justified not applying the presumptions.

propositions.text: The trial judge did not misinterpret the reasonable doubt standard or base findings on speculation, contrary to the majority's view.
propositions.quote: I cannot agree with the majority that the trial judge misinterpreted the reasonable doubt standard and that his findings were based on “speculation”

propositions.text: The accused only needed to raise a reasonable doubt about improper operation of the breathalyzer affecting reliability, not about exceeding the legal limit or result accuracy.
propositions.quote: The reasonable doubt simply had to relate to improper operation of the breathalyzer that could affect the reliability of the results.

propositions.text: The evidence in this case was not theoretical.
propositions.quote: On this point, the evidence adduced in the instant case was not “theoretical”.

paragraphs.summary: The court disagrees with the majority, clarifies the reasonable doubt standard, and finds the evidence was not theoretical.

propositions.text: The majority concedes that improper operation evidence may raise reasonable doubt about reliability in some circumstances.
propositions.quote: the majority concedes that, in certain circumstances, evidence of improper operation may in itself raise a reasonable doubt about the reliability of the results

propositions.text: Assessing sufficiency of evidence is for the trier of fact, as it involves evidence assessment.
propositions.quote: this is a matter for the trier of fact to decide, since it involves assessing the sufficiency of the evidence

propositions.text: Cites cases supporting that sufficiency of evidence is for the trier of fact.
propositions.quote: see Sunbeam Corporation (Canada) Ltd. v. The Queen, [1969] S.C.R. 221, at p. 231; Lampard v. The Queen, [1969] S.C.R. 373, at pp. 380‑81; Schuldt v. The Queen, [1985] 2 S.C.R. 592, at p. 608

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the majority concedes improper operation evidence may suffice, and affirms sufficiency is for the trier of fact, citing case law.

propositions.text: Mr. Cyr-Langlois adduced relevant evidence of improper operation, and the trial judge found it sufficient to raise reasonable doubt about reliability.
propositions.quote: Mr. Cyr‑Langlois adduced relevant evidence concerning the improper operation of the breathalyzer and the trial judge found that that evidence was sufficient to raise a reasonable doubt about the reliability of the results.

propositions.text: The Court should not intervene.
propositions.quote: This Court should therefore not intervene.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the evidence sufficient to raise reasonable doubt and decides not to intervene.

propositions.text: Constable Boissonneault stated that procedures include a 20-minute observation period to ensure no physiological reactions affect test reliability.
propositions.quote: Constable Boissonneault, the qualified technician, himself stated that the procedures prescribed by the École nationale de police du Québec include a 20‑minute observation period.

propositions.text: This testimony was sufficient to show a procedure exists for ensuring test reliability; no need to file the manual or have expert corroboration.
propositions.quote: This testimony was more than sufficient to show that a procedure exists for ensuring the reliability of the test results. There was no need to file the training manual of the École nationale de police du Québec, to which the witness referred, or to have an expert testify to corroborate what the witness had said.

paragraphs.summary: Constable Boissonneault testified about the observation procedure, and the court finds this testimony sufficient without needing manuals or expert corroboration.

propositions.text: Cross-examination showed Mr. Cyr-Langlois was not observed during the prescribed period to ensure reliability.
propositions.quote: Constable Boissonneault’s cross‑examination also tends to show that Mr. Cyr‑Langlois was not observed during the prescribed period to ensure that no physiological reaction affected the reliability of the results.

propositions.text: Constable Boissonneault did not observe the accused himself; Constable Cousineau did, but could not confirm continuous observation.
propositions.quote: The qualified technician stated that he had not observed the accused himself because he had been busy preparing the breathalyzer. Another police officer, Constable Cousineau, did so instead. However, Constable Boissonneault could not confirm that his colleague had observed the accused continuously during the 20‑minute period preceding the breathalyzer test.

propositions.text: There was a period when Mr. Cyr-Langlois was alone and unobserved, so it was unknown if he burped.
propositions.quote: there was a certain amount of time during which Constable Cousineau was unable to determine whether Mr. Cyr‑Langlois burped, since Mr. Cyr‑Langlois was alone in a soundproof room exercising his right to counsel.

propositions.text: The trial judge could find the technician’s testimony sufficient to raise reasonable doubt about compliance with the observation period.
propositions.quote: the trial judge could certainly find that the qualified technician’s testimony was sufficient to raise a reasonable doubt about compliance with the prescribed observation period.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds evidence showed the accused was not properly observed, supporting reasonable doubt about compliance with the observation period.

propositions.text: It was open to the trial judge to find the accused adduced evidence of improper operation affecting reliability, not just a possible deficiency.
propositions.quote: it was open to the trial judge to find that Mr. Cyr‑Langlois had adduced evidence tending to show improper operation of the breathalyzer that could affect the reliability of the results, and not “simply to show that a deficiency is possible”.

propositions.text: This is not conjecture or speculation, as the technician did not follow procedure or ensure no physiological reaction occurred.
propositions.quote: this is neither “conjecture” nor “speculation” (majority reasons, at para. 16), since, according to the evidence adduced, the qualified technician administered the tests without faithfully following the prescribed procedure and without ensuring, as he was required to do, that the accused did not have any physiological reaction that could distort the results.

propositions.text: The trial judge could have a reasonable doubt about the reliability of the results.
propositions.quote: The trial judge could therefore have a reasonable doubt about their reliability.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the trial judge could reasonably find improper operation evidence, not mere speculation, and thus have reasonable doubt about reliability.

propositions.text: At that point, the accused had discharged his burden under s. 258(1)(c) Cr. C. and did not have to adduce more evidence.
propositions.quote: At that point, the accused had discharged his burden under s. 258(1) (c) Cr. C. and did not have to adduce any other evidence.

propositions.text: Hogue J.A. wrote the trial judge was entitled not to extend the benefit of the presumptions to the prosecution and did not have to require more from the accused.
propositions.quote: the first instance judge was entitled not to extend the benefit of the presumptions to the prosecution. He did not have to require anything further from the accused.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the accused met his burden and, as Hogue J.A. held, the trial judge did not need to require more evidence from him.

propositions.text: Requiring the accused to testify about alcohol consumption and physiological reactions would violate the right to remain silent and be presumed innocent.
propositions.quote: it would be contrary to the right to remain silent and the right to be presumed innocent to require an accused to testify about his or her alcohol consumption and physiological reactions

propositions.text: The majority’s approach shifts the obligation to the accused to observe and report on himself, which is not justified.
propositions.quote: the majority’s approach shifts the obligation to the accused to observe himself or herself, make note of every physiological reaction and then testify about this, failing which the improper operation of the breathalyzer will be presumed to be of no consequence.

propositions.text: It is the state’s responsibility to ensure compliance with conditions for accurate results, not the accused’s.
propositions.quote: It is the state’s responsibility, not that of the accused, to ensure compliance with the requisite conditions for obtaining accurate results.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds requiring the accused to testify about consumption or reactions violates rights and that ensuring accuracy is the state's responsibility.

propositions.text: The majority suggests consistent test results tend to show non-compliance had no impact and confirm reliability.
propositions.quote: the majority suggests that the relative consistency of the two test results — among other evidence — tends to show that failure to comply with the observation period had no impact in this case, and thus tends to confirm the reliability of the results

propositions.text: Even if true, the onus was on the Crown to prove this, for example by technician or expert testimony, which it did not do.
propositions.quote: the onus was on the Crown to prove it, for example by having the qualified technician or an expert testify on this point. The Crown did not do so, however, and it must accept the consequences.

propositions.text: The presumptions of accuracy and identity in s. 258(1)(c) Cr. C. were no longer justified and had to be discarded.
propositions.quote: The application of the presumptions of accuracy and identity in s. 258(1) (c) Cr. C. was no longer justified, and the presumptions therefore had to be discarded.

propositions.text: In the absence of other evidence, the trial judge had no choice but to acquit Mr. Cyr-Langlois.
propositions.quote: In the absence of any other evidence showing that Mr. Cyr‑Langlois was guilty, the trial judge had no choice but to acquit him.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Crown failed to prove reliability despite consistent results, so presumptions were discarded and acquittal was required.

propositions.text: Even if agreeing with the Crown that more evidence was needed from the accused, the court would hesitate to order a new trial.
propositions.quote: even if I agreed with the Crown’s position that the accused had to introduce the qualified technician’s training manual in evidence and to testify about his alcohol consumption and physiological reactions, I would hesitate to order a new trial in this case.

propositions.text: An intervener pointed out the prosecution’s position on appeal differed from its position at trial.
propositions.quote: As pointed out by an intervener, the Association québécoise des avocats et avocates de la défense, the position taken by the prosecution on appeal is clearly different from the one it took at trial.

paragraphs.summary: The court would hesitate to order a new trial since the prosecution's appellate position differed from its trial position, as an intervener noted.

propositions.text: The Crown prosecutor did not argue at trial that technician testimony was insufficient or that manuals or accused testimony were required.
propositions.quote: The Crown prosecutor never argued before the trial judge that the qualified technician’s testimony could not be sufficient in law to counter the presumptions in s. 258(1) (c) Cr. C. He did not submit that it was necessary to introduce evidence of the recommended procedures by filing the relevant training or instruction manuals (in fact, he seemed to object to the filing of those manuals). Most importantly, he did not argue that the accused had to testify about his alcohol consumption and physiological reactions (such as burping) because otherwise there could be no reasonable doubt about the reliability of the results.

propositions.text: The prosecutor’s position at trial was that the accused was observed for a sufficient period in the circumstances.
propositions.quote: Rather, the prosecutor’s position was that Constables Boissonneault and Cousineau had observed the accused for a period of time that was sufficient in the circumstances.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Crown did not argue at trial for more evidence from the accused, but instead claimed sufficient observation occurred.

propositions.text: Ordering a new trial would give the Crown a second chance based on new arguments, contrary to the double jeopardy principle.
propositions.quote: To order a new trial would therefore be to give the Crown a second chance to have Mr. Cyr‑Langlois convicted, on the basis of arguments that were made for the first time on appeal. In my view, such a result would be contrary to the double jeopardy principle

propositions.text: Cites cases supporting the double jeopardy principle.
propositions.quote: see, for example, R. v. Varga (1994), 90 C.C.C. (3d) 484 (Ont. C.A.), at p. 494; R. v. Knight, 2015 ABCA 24, at para. 22 (CanLII); R. v. Suarez‑Noa, 2017 ONCA 627, 139 O.R. (3d) 508, at paras. 30‑35; R. v. Penno, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 865, at pp. 895‑96; R. v. Vaillancourt (1995), 105 C.C.C. (3d) 552 (Que. C.A.); R. v. Patel, 2017 ONCA 702, 356 C.C.C. (3d) 187, at paras. 34 and 58‑61; Wexler v. The King, [1939] S.C.R. 350, at pp. 353‑56

paragraphs.summary: The court finds a new trial would violate double jeopardy by giving the Crown a second chance based on new arguments, citing supporting cases.

propositions.text: The trial judge made no reviewable error in finding the accused raised reasonable doubt about improper operation affecting results, countering the presumptions.
propositions.quote: the trial judge made no reviewable error in finding that Mr. Cyr‑Langlois had raised a reasonable doubt about improper operation of the breathalyzer that could affect the results and that the presumptions of accuracy and identity in s. 258(1) (c) Cr. C. had therefore been countered.

propositions.text: Hogue J.A. agreed the trial judge did not have to require anything further from the accused.
propositions.quote: I agree with Hogue J.A. that the trial judge [translation] “did not have to require anything further from the accused” (para. 50; see also the reasons of Chamberland J.A., at paras. 60‑61).

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no reviewable error by the trial judge, agreeing with Hogue J.A. that nothing more was required from the accused.

propositions.text: The majority’s approach unduly limits defences based on improper operation that justify the evidentiary scheme for over-limit offences under s. 1 of the Charter.
propositions.quote: the majority’s approach unduly limits the defences based on improper operation of a breathalyzer that in fact make it possible to justify the evidentiary scheme applicable to offences involving driving with a blood alcohol level over the legal limit under s. 1 of the Charter .

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the majority's approach unduly limits improper operation defences that justify the evidentiary scheme under s. 1 of the Charter.

propositions.text: The majority’s reasons are based on arguments the Crown made for the first time on appeal, making a new trial inappropriate.
propositions.quote: the majority’s reasons are essentially based on arguments that the Crown made for the first time on appeal. It would be all the more inappropriate, in the circumstances, to order a new trial.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds a new trial inappropriate since the majority's reasons rely on arguments raised by the Crown only on appeal.

propositions.text: For all these reasons, I would dismiss the appeal.
propositions.quote: For all these reasons, I would dismiss the appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes by stating it would dismiss the appeal.
